title: Montana’s new “right to try” law can’t come soon enough for some
gist: A Montana father seeking an unapproved intranasal creatine drug for his three-year-old son with creatine transporter deficiency shows why the state's new right-to-try rules matter and why they may not work: the French developer, Ceres Brain Therapeutics, has only mouse data and an unpublished 48-person phase I, cannot use FDA expanded access because its manufacturing is non-compliant, and refuses to apply in Montana for fear of antagonizing the FDA. The family's fallback is an offshore clinic in Próspera, Honduras.

insights.claim: A three-year-old boy diagnosed at around two and a half with creatine transporter deficiency — a rare condition in which the brain and muscles lack the energy they need to develop — has no cure available and no prescribable option.
insights.so_what: Illustrates the untreated-rare-disease demand that gives state right-to-try laws their political momentum.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Parental urgency is driven by a biological deadline rather than by prognosis: early childhood brain plasticity means a treatment arriving in a few years may be worth far less than one arriving now.
insights.so_what: Time-sensitive windows in pediatric neurology make patients price-insensitive and regulation-tolerant, which is precisely the demand profile these clinics will serve.
insights.locator: DeVault is worried that will be too late
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Demand is intense enough that a single family treats one early-stage, animal-and-healthy-volunteer-only drug as its one shot.
insights.so_what: Willingness to pay for unproven assets is effectively unbounded in rare pediatric disease, which is what makes unregulated pricing lucrative.
insights.quote: I look at this, and I’m like, that is my one shot for Brody
insights.locator: The drug has not been tested in people with CTD
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: The asset: an early-stage intranasal creatine therapy

insights.claim: Ceres Brain Therapeutics is developing a nasal-spray treatment designed to bypass the defective creatine transporter and deliver creatine directly to the brain, with promising results so far only in mice.
insights.so_what: Defines exactly how thin the evidence base is for a drug already being sought by patients — mouse efficacy plus healthy-volunteer dosing.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The company recently completed a phase I trial testing various doses in 48 healthy adult volunteers, but that trial has not yet been published and the drug has never been tested in patients with the condition or in children.
insights.so_what: Unpublished phase I data in healthy adults is the actual evidentiary floor that Montana-style laws treat as sufficient for sale.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The planned phase II trial will cover both creatine transporter deficiency and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis but will run in France, effectively excluding US patients such as this family.
insights.so_what: Trial geography, not just trial timing, creates the access gap that offshore and state-level clinics are being built to fill.
insights.locator: Joudinaud is planning a phase II trial
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: Why the FDA's own compassionate route is closed here

insights.claim: The company cannot supply the drug under the FDA's expanded access scheme because the drug is not registered with the FDA and is currently manufactured in a way that does not comply with FDA regulations.
insights.so_what: Manufacturing compliance, not regulatory willingness, is the hidden gate on compassionate access — and it is a capex problem small biotechs often cannot solve.
insights.locator: Ceres can’t make the drug available
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Even if the phase II trial succeeds and the drug is ultimately approved, it is unlikely to reach the US market for at least a few years.
insights.so_what: The multi-year approval lag is the structural gap that alternative access markets monetize.
insights.locator: Even if that phase II trial is successful
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Efforts to extract a written FDA promise that companies participating in Montana's program will not be penalized during later approval have made no progress.
insights.so_what: Absent FDA cover, participation stays limited to firms indifferent to their FDA relationship — a self-selecting and lower-quality supply pool.
insights.locator: DeVault has been pleading with FDA staffers
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: Montana's pathway and its offshore competitor

insights.claim: Montana's framework arrived in three steps — a 2015 terminal-illness right-to-try law, a 2023 expansion to non-terminal patients whose drugs have cleared phase I, and a second law clarifying how clinics can sell and administer those treatments — with the implementing rules finalized only last weekend.
insights.so_what: The regulatory scaffolding is now complete, so activity from here is operational rather than legislative.
insights.locator: Montana has had a “right to try” law
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: An experimental treatment review board has been established and is set to review its first two applications in the coming weeks.
insights.so_what: A near-dated catalyst: the first approvals will set the de facto evidentiary bar for everything that follows.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The developer is reluctant to apply in Montana despite calling the setup very interesting, very pragmatic, and suitable for its drug, because of fear of getting on the wrong side of the FDA.
insights.so_what: Supply-side reluctance, not patient demand, is what will throttle the Montana market's growth.
insights.locator: Ceres could also apply to Montana’s ETRB
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: With Montana stalled for this family, the fallback is Próspera, a private city and special economic zone in Roatán, Honduras, where a clinic already sells unproven stem-cell and gene therapies.
insights.so_what: Montana is competing directly with offshore jurisdictions for the same patients; whichever clears applications fastest captures the flow.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Scientists, bioethicists, and health law experts caution that phase I clinical trials do not prove a drug is safe and certainly do not prove efficacy, and many have warned specifically against offshore clinics.
insights.so_what: The expert consensus is the standing reputational risk that a single bad outcome would convert into political reversal.
insights.locator: Even when it comes to Montana
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: A Harvard drug-regulation professor frames the objection in consumer-protection terms: patients deserve rigorous assessment so they understand what they are getting into and what they are paying their money for.
insights.so_what: Reframing the debate around payment rather than access is the strongest line of attack on the commercial model.
insights.quote: Patients who want these kinds of treatments deserve them to be rigorously assessed so that [they] can better understand what they’re getting themselves into, and what they’re paying their hard-earned money for.
insights.locator: When I spoke to Aaron Kesselheim
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The counterargument that will drive further liberalization is pure consumer autonomy — that an adult free to gamble away his savings or buy a firearm should be free to buy an unproven treatment for his child.
insights.so_what: This libertarian framing travels well politically and predicts more states copying Montana regardless of expert objections.
insights.quote: I’m capable of going to Vegas right now … blowing it all on the poker table, [or] I can go to the gun shop and buy a silenced [semi-automatic rifle]
insights.locator: But DeVault pushes back on these arguments
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
